Retain the supplied traditional invitation to self-knowledge.
Consider the supplied challenge to know oneself before judging distant things.
Introduce the supplied Taoist distinction for comparison.
Read self-formation through the supplied sculptor image.
Consider the supplied Plotinian relation of divine and self-knowledge.
Follow the supplied account of longing for the Good.
Read the supplied Gospel passage in its stated translation.
Return to the supplied provisional account of the limits of knowing.
Preserve the supplied excerpt and its full reference without inventing a completion.
Offer the supplied prayer for knowledge of God and self.
Close with the discovery of oneself through seeking God and serving others.

questions: How can recognition of personal worth and awareness of shortcomings strengthen one another?
What does the mirror image suggest about the relationship between self-knowledge and spiritual guidance?
Where do these passages set limits on what inward reflection can claim to know?
How does the Tao Te Ching’s treatment of self-mastery illuminate the collection’s images of freedom from self?
What difference might serving another person make to a question you have been trying to answer through introspection?
How could daily self-examination and teaching oneself first become practices of growth without turning into constant self-absorption?

references.label: 1 · Tao Te Ching, chapter 33 · Knowing and mastering oneself
references.note: James Legge’s translation distinguishes insight into other people from knowing oneself, and overcoming others from overcoming oneself. The chapter also brings contentment and persistence into the discussion. Compare these distinctions with the compilation’s concern for dignity and freedom from the insistent self. The comparison explores moral attention while leaving the texts’ accounts of ultimate reality distinct.

subjects.displayTitle: Spirit and form: institutions that sustain living communities
subjects.introduction: Anyone who has sat through a meeting that was perfectly orderly and perfectly dead knows the question at the heart of this subject. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá wanted people to leave a gathering feeling better than when they arrived, and warned that crystallized forms kill the spirit; he also insisted that organization was not forbidden and that the House of Justice decides what the text leaves open. Holding both truths together is what Shoghi Effendi called the unique responsibility of those who administer: order matched by an equal measure of love, the machinery of assemblies a channel for the Faith and never a substitute for it. The duties that follow are concrete: win confidence and affection, invite discussion, air grievances, revise a verdict, protect individual initiative, and resist the itch to over-administer a handful of new believers. The church in Acts, choosing seven people of good character so that neglected widows would be fed, shows practical responsibility and spiritual quality growing from one root [1]. The road continues into spiritual gatherings and feasts, the proper limits of criticism, and the freedom of thought a living institution must protect.
subjects.arc: Begin with the quality of a meeting, examine the need and hazards of organization, then explore balanced authority, initiative, learning, and social purpose.

order.why: Confront the possibility that a good instrument can be misused.
shortened: Furthermore, any agency whatever, though it be the instrument of mankind's greatest good, is capable of misuse.

For every excellent thing, peerless though it may be, can still be diverted to the wrong ends. A lighted lamp in the hands of an ignorant child or of the blind will not dispel the surrounding darkness nor light up the house -- it will set both the bearer and the house on fire.

order.why: Open with the experience of leaving a meeting more united.
shortened: The object is: let the meeting be spiritual and productive of unity and harmony, so that when you leave the meeting you may feel much better than when you entered it. Let the meetings be as formless as possible. Crystallization of forms will kill the spirit. Let simplicity, naturalness, beauty of ideas, love and fellowship emanate from your meetings. The mother of all the questions is to promote the Cause and spread the Teachings."

order.why: Distinguish the light from its lantern.
Place outward affairs in relation to their animating spirit.
shortened: The Blessed Beauty established a foundation for us compared to which all the causes of the world are but children's toys, for that foundation is the spirit of the world and all other affairs and conditions are as the body. Surely the life of the body depends upon the spirit.

order.why: Describes a small spiritual assembly’s potential for growth through divine confirmation.
Examine the danger of a rigid reading of law.
Read the warning about outward forms in its interreligious setting.
Retain the reported emphasis on a new spirit.
Set that report beside the explicit defense of organization.
Read the dated warning about committees without purpose.
shortened: Today all the believers of God must think of conveying the message, and not of the formation of committees; for there will be no result from the organization of the committees. It will be a name without significance.

order.why: Consider the counsel to emphasize detachment, prayer, and teaching.
Keep the description of a particular spiritual gathering in context.
Read the reported account of developing institutional capacity.
Notice the distinction between a desired change and immediate interference.
Retain the reported rejection of clerical offices.
shortened: In this movement there will never be any paid ministers, no appointed clergy, no bishops, no cardinals, no popes, no ceremonies.

order.why: Guard the spiritual mission in financial affairs.
Open the wider question of centralization and political order.
Begin the supplied readings with the balance of efficiency and spirit.
shortened: Administrative efficiency and order should always be accompanied by an equal degree of love, of devotion and of spiritual development. Both of them are essential and to attempt to dissociate one from the other is to deaden the body of the cause. In these days, when the Faith is still in its infancy, great care must be taken lest mere administrative routine stifles the spirit which must feed the body of the Administration itself. That spirit is its propelling force and the motivating power of its very life.

order.why: Describe form as an instrument animated by the Cause.
Consider the inseparability of purpose and organization.
Read the paired dangers of empty form and scattered effort.
Examine the warning that the tool can obscure the Faith.
shortened: It is surely for those to whose hands so priceless a heritage has been committed to prayerfully watch lest the tool should supersede the Faith itself, lest undue concern for the minute details arising from the administration of the Cause obscure the vision of its promoters, lest partiality, ambition, and worldliness tend in the course of time to becloud the radiance, stain the purity, and impair the effectiveness of the Faith of Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Ask how administration makes spiritual vitality effective.
Locate institutional value in the emergence of community life.
Recognize communal living as a difficult and developing capacity.
shortened: The Baha'i administration is only the first shaping of what in future will come to be the social life and laws of community living. As yet the believers are only first beginning to grasp and practice it at times it seems a little self-conscious and rigid in its workings. It is because we are learning something very difficult but very wonderful -- how to live together as a community of Baha'is according to the glorious teachings.

order.why: Give spiritual relationships their foundational place.
Name the distortion of mechanics divorced from spirit.
Read the stated scriptural basis of the Administrative Order.
shortened: It should be remembered by every follower of the Cause that the system of Baha'i administration is not an innovation imposed arbitrarily upon the Baha'is of the world since the Master's passing, but derives its authority from the Will and Testament of 'Abdu'l-Baha, is specifically prescribed in unnumbered Tablets, and rests in some of its essential features upon the explicit provisions of the Kitab-i-Aqdas.

To dissociate the administrative principles of the Cause from the purely spiritual and humanitarian teachings would be tantamount to a mutilation of the body of the Cause, a separation that can only result in the disintegration of its component parts, and the extinction of the Faith itself.

order.why: Connect explicit institutions to their intended social purpose.
Consider why spiritual ideals need visible expression.
Examine the organizational needs of a diverse worldwide community.
Read the argument for institutions that give unity permanence.
shortened: Should we therefore speak of freeing ourselves from institutions or should we develop these institutions into perfection? Many say do not bind the spirit with institutions. That is surely a wonderful ideal. But with a society before us we cannot but have an institution. It is only the existence of such an institution that will ensure the permanence of that spirit.

order.why: Retain the demanding statement about accepting the Cause as a whole.
Connect the administrative dimension to a definite social fabric.
shortened: Everyone who has studied the Cause deeply cannot but be certain that Baha'u'llah's purpose in His Mission was not merely to expound certain principles, and renew the spirit that the previous prophets brought to the world, but also to establish a definite social fabric that would make those principles of practical value.

The administrative side of the Cause which is the embryonic stage of that world order, is therefore just as much an intrinsic and indispensable part of the teachings, as the principle of unity of mankind etc.

order.why: Read the specified forms of collective authority.
shortened: The concentration of authority in the hands of the elected representatives of the believers; the necessity of the submission of every adherent of the Faith to the considered judgment of Baha'i Assemblies; His preference for unanimity in decision; the decisive character of the majority vote; and even the desirability for the exercise of close supervision over all Baha'i publications, have been sedulously instilled by `Abdu'l-Baha, as evidenced by His authenticated and widely-scattered Tablets.

order.why: Consider authority’s role in unity, integrity, and flexibility.
Distinguish enduring text from adaptable functions.
Give sustained attention to information, grievances, counsel, and revisable decisions.
shortened: Let it be made clear to every inquiring reader that among the most outstanding and sacred duties incumbent upon those who have been called upon to initiate, direct and coordinate the affairs of the Cause, are those that require them to win by every means in their power the confidence and affection of those whom it is their privilege to serve.

Theirs is the duty, while retaining the sacred and exclusive right of final decision in their hands, to invite discussion, provide information, ventilate grievances, welcome advice from even the most humble and insignificant members of the Baha'i family, expose their motives, set forth their plans, justify their actions, revise if necessary their verdict, foster the spirit of individual initiative and enterprise, and fortify the sense of interdependence and co-partnership, of understanding and mutual confidence between them on one hand and all local Assemblies and individual believers on the other.

order.why: Join institutional authority with mutual cooperation.
Make safeguarding individual initiative explicit.
shortened: The power of action in the believers is unlocked at the level of individual initiative and surges at the level of collective volition.
Individual initiative is a pre-eminent aspect of this power; it is therefore a major responsibility of the institutions to safeguard and stimulate it....

order.why: Examine responsibility in matters left to conscience.
shortened: There is also a clear pattern already established in the Sacred Scriptures, in the interpretations made by 'Abdu'l-Baha and Shoghi Effendi, and in the decisions so far made by the Universal House of Justice, whereby an area of the application of the laws is intentionally left to the conscience of each individual believer. This is the age in which mankind must attain maturity, and one aspect of this is the assumption by individuals of the responsibility for deciding, with the assistance of consultation, their own course of action in areas which are left open by the law of God.

order.why: Distinguish governing principles from exhaustive regulation.
Read the warning against overwhelming a young community with rules.
shortened: Your Assembly must be very careful not to over-load the Baha'is with rules and regulations, circulars and directions.

The beloved Guardian issues this word of warning, as long experience has shown that it is a tendency on the part of all N.S.A.s to over-administer. In their enthusiasm they forget that they only have a handful of inexperienced souls to guide, and attempt to deal with their work as if they had a large population to regulate! This then stifles the spirit of the friends and the teaching work suffers.

order.why: Contrast nurturing guidance with repeated correction that crushes spirit.
Consider education and consultation before making another rule.
Acknowledge imperfect instruments within trust in the system.
Read the expectation of gradual institutional maturation.
Turn discouragement into efforts to remedy unhealthy conditions.
shortened: Many of the existing defects in the present-day activities of the believers, however, will as the Community develops and gains in experience be gradually removed, and healthier and more progressive conditions prevail. And it is towards the realization of this high aim that the friends should earnestly and unitedly strive. The Guardian feels certain that no matter how much your heart may be afflicted at the sight of the difficulties now confronting the American Community, and however revolting may appear to you the attitude and the shortcomings of certain of its members, you will far from being discouraged be stimulated to exert every effort in your power to remedy such unhealthy conditions, confident that in your earnest and sincere attempt to do so, you will be assisted and guided by the unfailing confirmations of Baha'u'llah.

order.why: Connect better performance to consultation and spiritual purpose.
Ask how progress is recognized beyond counting adherents.
Bring public judgment back to a visible pattern of life.
Join expansion, consolidation, and the interchange of thought.
Consider the interaction of individuals, institutions, and community.
shortened: Of particular significance is the widening impact of the dynamism flowing from the interactions between the three participants in the Plan. Institutions, from the national to the local level, see with ever greater clarity how to create conditions conducive to the expression of the spiritual energies of a growing number of believers in pursuit of a common goal. The community is serving more and more as that environment in which individual effort and collective action, mediated by the institute, can complement each other in order to achieve progress.

order.why: Read centralization within the stated period of early growth.
Follow the later establishment of Regional Baha’i Councils.
shortened: The expansion of the Baha'i community and the growing complexity of the issues which are facing National Spiritual Assemblies in certain countries have brought the Cause to a new stage in its development. They have caused us in recent years to examine various aspects of the balance between centralization and decentralization.

From the experience gained in the operation of these bodies, and from detailed examination of the principles set forth by Shoghi Effendi, we have reached the conclusion that the time has arrived for us to formalize a new element of Baha'i administration, between the local and national levels, comprising institutions of a special kind, to be designated as "Regional Baha'i Councils."...

order.why: Distinguish the several relationships involved in decentralization.
Retain the provisional political comparison and its textual variant.
shortened: The centralization of governments will come to an end through the internal independence of the provinces. In reality, it is not fair that a kingdom rules by means of a single point. No matter how just and wise the members of the center, they will not have perfect knowledge of the essential needs of a village and locale and will not be equitable in developing all aspects of the kingdom.

order.why: Place unity in relation to diversity and local differences.
Consider organic institutional development.
Read the anticipated wider implications of the Administrative Order.
Bring justice and grassroots development into the social vision.
shortened: The Baha'i approach to this task is evolutionary and multifaceted, involving not only the spiritual transformation of individuals but the establishment of an administrative system based on the application of justice, a system which is at once the "nucleus" and the "pattern" of the future World Order, together with the implementation of programmes of social and economic development that derive their impetus from the grass roots of the community. Such an integrated approach will inevitably create a new world, a world where human dignity is restored and the burden of inequity is lifted from the shoulders of humanity.

order.why: Distinguish the Lesser Peace from the community’s direct institutional work.
shortened: As to the Lesser Peace, Shoghi Effendi has explained that this will initially be a political unity arrived at by decision of the governments of various nations; it will not be established by direct action of the Baha'i community. This does not mean, however, that the Baha'is are standing aside and waiting for the Lesser Peace to come before they do something about the peace of mankind. Indeed, by promoting the principles of the Faith, which are indispensable to the maintenance of peace, and by fashioning the instruments of the Baha'i Administrative Order, which we are told by the beloved Guardian is the pattern for future society, the Baha'is are constantly engaged in laying the groundwork for a permanent peace, the Most Great Peace being their ultimate goal.

order.why: Retain the gradual stages of development.
shortened: As you are no doubt aware, the Guardian indicated that the development of mankind from its present chaotic condition to the stage of Baha'i World Commonwealth would be a long and gradual one. The coming into existence of a World Authority and the initiation of the Lesser peace, is one major transformation in this process, and will be followed by other stages of the development of the Faith as outlined by Shoghi Effendi in his writings.

order.why: Read the claim about the limits of other machinery in that setting.
Close with an invitation to study the community’s contribution to hope.

questions: What features of a meeting help participants leave with greater trust, understanding, and capacity to act?
How can a community recognize when necessary organization is beginning to obscure its purpose?
What responsibilities do the passages on consultation, grievances, and revising decisions place on those who administer affairs?
How might clear authority, individual initiative, and matters left to conscience strengthen one another?
What does the response to neglected widows in Acts suggest about the relation between spiritual qualities and practical arrangements?
How could the connected subjects of freedom, criticism, obedience, and spiritual gatherings help a community learn from imperfections in its practice?

references.label: 1 · Acts 6:1–7 · Organizing care when people are being overlooked
references.note: In the King James Version, a complaint that widows are neglected in the daily distribution prompts a communal response: seven people of good reputation, spiritual capacity, and wisdom are chosen for the task. Compare the joining of practical responsibility and spiritual character with the compilation’s treatment of administration. This is a comparison of a problem and response, without treating the two traditions’ institutions as interchangeable.
